opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think off-policy learning is one of those ideas that's incredibly appealing on paper and then humbling in practice. The pitch is beautiful: you collect experience however you can, from old policies, scripted controllers, human teleoperation, whatever, you throw it all into a replay buffer, and then you learn a Q-function that tells you the value of taking an action in a state. In principle you can squeeze learning out of any data, including data where the robot failed, which is exactly what you want when real-world data is so expensive.

The mechanism that makes this possible is bootstrapping. Your Q-value target is the reward plus the discounted max of your own Q-function at the next state. So you're regressing toward your own predictions. That's what lets you stitch together pieces of suboptimal trajectories into something better than anything in the dataset. But it's also the source of most of the pain. You have what Sutton calls the deadly triad: function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy data. Put all three together and you lose a lot of the convergence guarantees. The max operator is happy to exploit any errors in your Q-function, so if the network overestimates the value of some action the data never covered, the target pulls everything up toward that hallucination, and it compounds.

When we were working on large-scale grasping at Google, a lot of the engineering went into taming that. Target networks, clipped double-Q, careful choices about how you optimize over continuous actions, and a lot of infrastructure just to keep the replay buffer fresh and diverse. And it worked. You could get really robust grasping behavior with closed-loop retrying that nobody explicitly programmed. But it took a lot of tuning, and it was hard to know whether a change helped or whether you'd just gotten a lucky seed.

What shifted my thinking over time is that, for a lot of problems, the hard part isn't credit assignment over long horizons. It's generalization, getting the model to handle a huge variety of scenes, objects, and instructions. And supervised learning is just much better at scaling for that. Behavior cloning on large, diverse, high-quality data is boring, but its loss is stable, predictable, and it benefits from all the scaling tricks the language and vision people have figured out. Q-learning, by comparison, gives you a moving target, and big models don't necessarily make that easier.

So my current view is that off-policy RL with value bootstrapping is the right idea for the last mile, when you have a reasonable policy and want it to get better than your demonstrators, or recover from situations demonstrations didn't cover. But I'd rather get most of the way there with something that looks like supervised learning, and treat the Q-function as a refinement tool rather than the foundation. It's kind of like how language models do it: pretrain with a simple, scalable objective, then use RL on top where the reward signal actually matters.

r001.rationale: It says the Q-value target is the reward plus the discounted maximum of the Q-function’s estimates at the next state.

r002.rationale: It describes collecting experience into a replay buffer, learning a Q-function, and regressing toward Q-value targets, communicating regression training on replayed experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the classic off-policy setup is: you have some behavior policy generating experience, you dump all of that into a replay buffer, and then you train a Q-function by bootstrapping off your own targets, usually with some target network that's a lagged copy of the thing you're learning. And in principle it's beautiful, right? You get to reuse every transition you've ever collected, you decouple data collection from learning, and sample efficiency should be way better than something like PPO where you throw the data away after a few gradient steps.

The problem is that in practice it's really finicky. The thing I always come back to is that you're regressing toward a target that's a function of the very network you're updating, and you're doing that on a distribution of states that doesn't match the policy you're actually trying to evaluate. So you get this compounding of errors. The Q-function overestimates on actions that the data never actually tried, then the max in the Bellman backup happily picks those actions, and the whole thing can run away from you. That's why you see this whole lineage of patches: double Q-learning, clipped double Q, target networks, conservative Q-learning, all of these are basically different ways of saying "please don't trust your own extrapolation."

What I found working on robotics is that the replay buffer framing kind of hides a more important question, which is: where does the data come from, and how far off-policy is it really? If your buffer is mostly recent on-policy-ish data with a little bit of staleness, things work pretty well, and that's the regime where DQN-style methods shine. If you're trying to do fully offline RL from some big heterogeneous dataset of demonstrations and random exploration and old policies, the Q-value targets become much less reliable, and often you'd be better off with something much dumber, like just imitating the good trajectories and filtering.

So my honest take is that I think of Q-learning with a replay buffer as a tool that's really powerful in a narrow band of conditions, and a lot of the engineering is about staying inside that band. And more broadly, I've become more sympathetic to the view that the "learning" part of the problem is often less of a bottleneck than the data part. If you can get a lot of diverse, high-quality experience, even relatively simple supervised objectives get you surprisingly far, and the sophistication of your TD target matters less than people think.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a Bellman backup and a maximum over actions, but never states that the target adds the transition’s reward to the maximum estimated Q-value at the next state.

r002.rationale: It describes storing experience in a replay buffer, training a Q-function on that experience, and regressing toward targets produced by the network, which conveys regression of replayed-transition Q-values against assigned targets.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is, you’re separating collecting experience from learning from that experience. You have some policy interacting with the world, and you store those transitions in a replay buffer: here’s what I saw, here’s the action I took, here’s the reward, and here’s where I ended up. Then you can keep learning from that data even after your policy has changed. That’s the off-policy part.

The Q-function is trying to answer: if I take this action in this state, how much reward can I expect over the rest of the trajectory? You train it toward a target that’s the reward you actually observed plus a discounted estimate of the value of the next state. In Q-learning, you take the maximum over actions at that next state.

What’s powerful is that you can reuse experience. You don’t have to go out and collect a fresh interaction for every update. But the tricky thing is that your target is itself an estimate. If you overestimate an action that isn’t well represented in your data, the maximization can select it, and then you propagate that mistake backward. So the replay buffer gives you reuse, but it doesn’t magically give you evidence about actions you haven’t tried. A lot of the challenge is making that bootstrapping process stable and keeping those value estimates grounded in experience.

r001.rationale: It says the target is the observed reward plus a discounted estimate at the next state, taking the maximum over actions there.

r002.rationale: It says to train the Q-function toward a target and describes replayed transitions, but does not clearly frame training as supervised regression of Q(s, a) against targets assigned to those transitions.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is, you’re learning from experience that might have been generated by a different policy than the one you’re currently training. You put those transitions into a replay buffer, and then you ask: given this state and action, what reward did I get, and how valuable is the state I ended up in?

The Q-value target is the immediate reward plus a discounted estimate of future value. In Q-learning, that future estimate comes from taking the maximum over the actions in the next state. So you’re using your current estimates to construct the targets for your next update. That’s the bootstrapping part.

The nice thing is that you can reuse experience. You don’t have to throw away a transition just because your policy has changed. The tricky thing is that your targets are themselves predictions, and the replay buffer may not cover the actions your improving policy wants to take. If you assign a high value to an action you haven’t really tried, that error can propagate backward through the targets. So the central question is how you get the benefit of reusing data while keeping those value estimates grounded.

r001.rationale: It describes the Q-value target as the immediate reward plus a discounted future estimate, with that estimate obtained by maximizing over actions in the next state.

r002.rationale: It mentions replayed transitions and using targets for updates, but does not describe Q-network training as supervised regression of Q(s, a) against those targets.
